questions.question: Sunlight passes through the air and warms the ground. The warm ground then gives off invisible infrared rays, which head upward toward space. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and a few other gases in the air keep the ground warmer than it would be without them. How do these greenhouse gases keep it warmer?
questions.answer: They absorb the rays and send part of them back down
choices: They absorb the rays and send part of them back down
They reflect the rays back down, as a mirror does
They trap all the rays, so none escape into space
They stop warm air rising, as a glass roof does
questions.context: A greenhouse gas molecule absorbs an infrared ray and soon gives the energy off again in any direction, so part of it heads back down to the ground and part goes on upward. Nothing bounces off the gases as light bounces off a mirror, and in the end Earth sends about as much energy out to space as it takes in from sunlight. A glass greenhouse works another way, mostly by keeping its warm air from rising and drifting off.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7; TEKS 8.11, NGSS MS-ESS3-5) teaches the greenhouse effect as gases trapping outgoing heat; the step a grade deeper than 7th is how they do it: absorbed, then sent out again, part back down.

questions.question: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air, yet the infrared rays given off by the warm ground pass through them almost untouched. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane, present in far smaller amounts, absorb those rays. What sets nitrogen and oxygen apart?
questions.answer: Their molecules are pairs of identical atoms
choices: Their molecules are pairs of identical atoms
Their molecules are lighter than water's or methane's
They are too unreactive to take in any energy
They are colourless, so the rays pass through them
questions.context: A nitrogen molecule (N2) is two nitrogen atoms and an oxygen molecule (O2) two oxygen atoms, and when such a pair vibrates its electric charge stays evenly spread, so it cannot catch infrared rays. Molecules with three or more atoms, such as H2O, CO2 and CH4, bend and stretch lopsidedly and so absorb them. Weight, colour and reactivity do not explain it: water and methane molecules are lighter than nitrogen's, all these gases are colourless, and oxygen is highly reactive.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7) names the greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour); why the air's main gases are not among them is the mechanism step, told with formulas the grade already reads (N2, O2, CO2, H2O).

questions.question: Eunice Foote set two matching glass cylinders, with thermometers inside them, in the sunshine in 1856. One cylinder was filled with carbon dioxide, and the other with ordinary air. She read the thermometers every few minutes, then took the cylinders out of the sunlight. What did she find?
questions.answer: The carbon dioxide grew hotter and stayed hot longer
choices: The carbon dioxide grew hotter and stayed hot longer
The ordinary air grew hotter and stayed hot longer
The two grew equally hot and cooled at the same rate
The carbon dioxide grew hotter but cooled more quickly
questions.context: Foote's carbon dioxide reached 125 degrees Fahrenheit, against 106 for ordinary air in her tests, and took many times as long to cool; she wrote that an atmosphere of that gas would give Earth a high temperature. Joseph Henry read her paper to a scientific meeting in Albany, New York, that August. Her cylinders took in the whole of sunlight, so they could not single out the infrared rays the ground gives off; John Tyndall's experiments did that three years later.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7) teaches that carbon dioxide traps heat; Foote's side-by-side cylinders are the first experiment that showed it, and middle-school lessons on the greenhouse effect (the AIP's Foote and Tyndall guide) use them.

questions.question: John Tyndall began measuring how gases absorb heat at the Royal Institution in London in 1859. He sent invisible rays from a copper cube of boiling water down a long brass tube to a detector at the far end. Nitrogen and oxygen let almost all the heat pass, yet ordinary air from his laboratory absorbed far more. Which of that air's gases did most of the absorbing?
choices: Its water vapour
Its carbon dioxide
Its methane
Its ozone
questions.context: Tyndall found that the water vapour in his laboratory air absorbed at least thirteen times as much heat as the dry air itself, which made it the strongest absorber among the air's gases. Carbon dioxide absorbed heat too, but there is far less of it in the air. He wrote that every change in the air's water vapour must change the climate.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7) names water vapour with carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases; Tyndall's tube is the classic experiment that measured gases absorbing heat.

questions.question: Svante Arrhenius, a Swedish chemist, worked through thousands of sums by hand and published the results in 1896. Using Samuel Langley's measurements of invisible heat rays from the Moon, he calculated how much warmer or colder each band of latitude would be with less carbon dioxide in the air, or with more. What puzzle had set him to work?
questions.answer: What had brought on the ice ages
choices: What had brought on the ice ages
Why cities are warmer than the countryside
Why Venus is far hotter than Earth
Why the poles are colder than the tropics
questions.context: No one had a good explanation of how Earth's climate could have turned cold enough for an ice age. Arrhenius found that cutting the air's carbon dioxide to a little over half would cool the middle latitudes by 4 to 5 degrees Celsius, enough for an ice age, and that doubling it would warm Earth by about 5 to 6 degrees. He called the work tedious calculations.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7) teaches the greenhouse gases and the natural causes of climate change; Arrhenius's 1896 calculation, with carbon dioxide as a cause of the ice ages, is the first estimate of how much the gas warms the planet.

questions.question: Many scientists of the 1950s expected the oceans to soak up nearly all the carbon dioxide given off by burning coal and oil. Charles David Keeling began measuring the gas in March 1958 at an observatory high on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii, standing on bare lava far from any continent. What had his readings shown by 1960?
questions.answer: The gas building up in the air, year after year
choices: The gas building up in the air, year after year
The gas holding steady, soaked up by the oceans
The gas slowly falling, taken in by plants and seas
The gas jumping up and down, with no clear pattern
questions.context: Keeling's first reading was 313 parts per million. The yearly average has risen every year since, and readings had reached about 430 parts per million by early 2026, the yearly rise having grown from about 0.7 to more than 2.5 parts per million. Roger Revelle and Hans Suess had already shown that the ocean's surface water takes up far less of the gas than a simple calculation predicts.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7) teaches that burning fuels releases greenhouse gases; the Keeling record from Mauna Loa is the measurement the grade's lessons use to show carbon dioxide rising.

questions.question: Charles David Keeling's carbon dioxide record from Mauna Loa does not climb smoothly. Every year the readings fall from about May until October, then climb again until the next May, a swing of about six parts per million. What causes this yearly zigzag?
questions.answer: Northern forests and fields growing, then dying back
choices: Northern forests and fields growing, then dying back
Southern forests and fields growing, then dying back
Polar sea ice freezing over, then melting away
The volcano below venting more, then venting less
questions.context: Most of Earth's land, and so most of its plants, lies in the northern half of the world. Through the northern spring and summer those plants take carbon dioxide from the air as they grow, and in autumn and winter dead leaves and plants decay and give it back. The southern half has far less land, and the record at the South Pole shows almost no yearly swing.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E8; TEKS 8.11C) teaches carbon moving between the air and living things by photosynthesis, respiration and decay; the Keeling zigzag is that exchange seen in the whole air.

questions.question: Carbon is always on the move between Earth's great stores, passing from one to another and back over time. Leaving aside the vast amount locked up in limestone and other rocks like it, which store holds the most carbon?
questions.answer: The oceans, dissolved in sea water
choices: The oceans, dissolved in sea water
Living things and the soil beneath them
Fossil fuels, such as coal and oil
The air, as carbon dioxide gas
questions.context: Sea water holds about 38,000 billion tonnes of carbon, some forty to fifty times as much as the air. Coal, oil and gas hold perhaps 5,000 to 10,000 billion tonnes, the soil 1,500 to 2,400 and living plants 450 to 650. Carbon moves between these stores all the time: plants take it from the air, breathing and decay return it, the sea dissolves it, and burning sends the carbon of fossil fuels, buried for millions of years, back into the air.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E8; TEKS 8.11C) teaches the carbon cycle's stores (air, living things, oceans, rocks and fossil fuels) and how carbon moves between them.

questions.question: Mount Tambora, a volcano on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia, exploded in April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history. Its cloud rose more than 40 kilometres, high into the stratosphere. The next year snow fell in New England in June, and crops failed across Europe. What in the cloud cooled the world?
questions.answer: Tiny droplets formed from its sulfur gas
choices: Tiny droplets formed from its sulfur gas
Fine ash formed from its shattered rock
Steam formed from the water in its magma
Carbon dioxide given off by its magma
questions.context: Tambora threw about 60 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it became a haze of tiny sulfuric acid droplets that reflected sunlight back into space for a year or more, and 1816 became the year without a summer. Ash falls out of the sky within days to weeks, and steam and carbon dioxide are greenhouse gases, which warm rather than cool.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (G8.E7; TEKS 8.11A) teaches volcanic eruptions as a natural cause of climate change whose gases cool the planet; Tambora's year without a summer is the classic case.
